query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Engineered multilayer HEA coatings exhibit superior resistance to time‐dependent plastic deformation because their coherent, compositionally or crystallographically tuned interfaces generate residual compressive stresses and act as effective dislocation barriers, thereby elevating the activation energy needed for dislocation motion and atomic diffusion during creep.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloy protective coatings fabricated as multilayers with alternating layers that differ in lattice parameters and/or slight compositional variations (designed to promote coherent interfaces) as deposited by sputtering or a similar method.
generation.intervention: Fabricate two sets of HEA coatings: one as a multilayer architecture with deliberately engineered coherent interfaces (via controlled layer thickness and mismatch) and one as a homogeneous (single‐layer) coating with the identical overall composition, then subject both to elevated-temperature, constant-stress creep testing.
generation.conditions: Testing under temperatures and stresses where time-dependent plastic (creep) deformation is typically activated (e.g., mid-to-high service temperatures of protective coatings), with layer thicknesses in the tens to hundreds of nanometers ensuring interface coherency.
generation.structural_mediator: The multilayer interfaces—where controlled lattice mismatch induces residual compressive stresses and interfacial coherency—that impede dislocation propagation and suppress atomic diffusion along the interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Dislocations generated during creep become pinned at the coherent interfaces; the induced residual compressive stresses further stabilize these interfaces and hinder both dislocation glide and climb. This combined barrier effect increases the effective activation energy for deformation and reduces strain accumulation, leading to lower creep rates compared to a homogeneous HEA coating.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature and stress conditions, the multilayer HEA coating will display lower steady-state creep rates, higher measured activation energies for creep, and a delayed onset of tertiary creep relative to the homogeneous single-phase coating.
generation.baseline: A homogeneous, single-phase HEA coating (of the same overall composition and thickness) lacking engineered multilayer interfaces.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under conditions where the multilayer architecture maintains coherent interfaces (layer thickness controlled to tens-hundreds of nanometers) and at temperatures sufficiently high for creep activation but below those that introduce secondary phase transformations or cause interface degradation.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines findings from MD simulations that attribute enhanced creep resistance in HEAs to effective phase (γ/γ′) interfaces [PMC12842692::web::019::3_3_difference_in_creep_resistance_betwe, PMC12842692::web::023::3_4_effect_of_lattice_misfit_on_the_cree] with experimental observations showing that modified boundary morphologies (e.g., serrated grain boundaries) reduce local strain concentrations [PMC9848264::web::017::discussion]. What is new here is extending these interfacial effects to multilayer coatings, whose interface-generated residual stress fields and dislocation blocking characteristics remain untested in this specific geometry. The magnitude of the effect and potential influences of layer thickness variations are yet uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples – multilayer HEA coatings with engineered coherent interfaces (variable layer thicknesses to enforce lattice misfit) and homogeneous single-layer HEA coatings with the same overall composition and thickness. Subject both groups to identical creep tests (constant stress and temperature) using in situ techniques (e.g., high-temperature synchrotron diffraction, in situ TEM creep) to track dislocation motion and interface behavior.
measurements: Steady-state creep rate and strain evolution over time
Activation energy for creep by fitting creep curves
In situ imaging of dislocation pile-up and interface strain fields
Residual stress mapping across the multilayer interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in creep rate or increased activation energy compared to the homogeneous coating, and/or if in situ imaging reveals negligible dislocation pile-up at the interfaces or absence of residual stress effects, then the hypothesis that coherent multilayer interfaces enhance creep resistance via dislocation blocking and residual compressive stress is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The preceding analyses clearly indicate that under identical creep conditions, the HESA exhibits a significantly lower creep rate than the HEA, thereby demonstrating superior creep resistance. This section elucidates the underlying reasons for this difference from the perspective of microstructural evolution. Figure 10 presents the creep deformation behavior of HESA under extreme conditions (1000 K and 2.5 GPa), with distinct phase identification via color coding: the γ matrix phase is shown in purple, and the γ′ precipitates are depicted in green. The microstructural evolution reveals continuous dislocation generation at GBs, followed by their subsequent propagation into grain interiors. As creep time progresses, additional slip systems become activated, leading to concurrent dislocation motion within the same grain. This results in the formation of parallel slip bands, which are clearly observed in Figure 10. One of the key features observed is the pronounced hindering effect of the γ/γ′ interface on dislocation motion. cited_evidence.text: As shown in Figure 13, all creep curves exhibit the typical three-stage behavior. Notably, the duration of the steady-state creep stage decreases with increasing |δ|. The relationship between creep life and |δ| is non-monotonic. Specifically, within the range of −0.1688% to −0.084%, creep life increases as |δ| increases. Conversely, within the range of −0.8075% to −0.1688%, creep life decreases as |δ| increases. The longest creep life is observed at δ = −0.1688%. To gain further insight into the underlying mechanisms, atomic strain distributions were analyzed, as shown in Figure 14. Figure 14a,b compare atomic strain maps of HESAs with negative (−0.1402%) and positive (0.1402%) lattice misfits. At t = 130 ps, the model with the negative lattice misfit (Figure 14a) exhibits lower atomic strain, suggesting enhanced resistance to deformation. This implies that a negative lattice misfit stabilizes the γ′ phase, strengthens the γ/γ′ interface, and impedes dislocation motion, thereby improving creep resistance. The intermediate-temperature creep behavior and microstructural evolution of CoCrFeNiMn HEA have been studied. Optical micrographs and TEM images of the dislocation substructure after creep deformation revealed the effects of dynamic recrystallization and dynamic precipitation on the deformation mechanisms. The following conclusions can be drawn:An obvious transition in stress exponent and average activation energy was observed: At low stresses, the values were approximately 5 to 6 and 268 kJ/mol, whereas at high-stress regions, the corresponding values were 8.9–14 and 380 kJ/mol. Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion is suggested as a possible rate-dominating mechanism at low stresses.At high stresses, obvious dynamic recrystallization occurred, leading to the refinement of average grain size. Simultaneously, nano-sized M23C6 carbides and the Cr-rich tetragonal σ phase were dynamically precipitated. High density of tangled and curved dislocation substructures was observed. In summary, indentation creep tests for reduced activity HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr HEAs were performed by static and dynamic loads at 298 K, 423 K and 573 K. The creep mechanism of the alloys were compared in terms of stress exponent and activation volume. Comparison of the creep resistance of the three systems was done based on creep displacement and activation energy. The following conclusions were drawn: The creep exponent was in the range of 20–140 and activation volume was in the range of 13–20b3, indicating that the time-dependent deformations for all alloys were dislocation dominated. The stress exponent decreased with increasing temperature owing to thermally activated dislocations and the reduction was sharper for HEAs compared to pure W. The creep exponent increased with increasing load (depth) leading to an apparent size effect due to a higher generation rate of dislocation and their entanglement at larger penetration depth. A higher diffusion/annihilation rate of dislocations near the free surface at a smaller depth may be another possible explanation. Both HT-1 and HT-2 samples have almost identical tensile strength and ductility at 25°C (Table 1 and Figure 6); ductile transgranular fractures were dominant at room temperature (Figure 7(a,c)). However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The initiation of creep damage of HT-1 sample was a result of vacancy coalescence on grain boundaries perpendicular to the loading direction and severe strain concentration at grain boundaries.
